utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber has not heard of any preliminaries to be raised. Therefore, we'll start with the testimony of the next witness, who will testify with face and voice distortion and pseudonym, which means that we have to briefly move into closed session to allow the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I'm calling you "Witness 401" because you have been granted protection measures, and I will now switch to English, and I would like you to take the solemn declaration, according to which you're going to say the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will testify with -- with protective measures. That is, we'll not call you by your own name. Your face is not visible; your own voice is not audible by the outside world, but apart from that your testimony is public. Now, if you ever feel that one of your answers might reveal your identity, please address me so that we can move into private session so as to avoid that your identity becomes known. I also welcome the representative of the French government, Ms. Bass, who is with you; and, as Ms. Bass knows, her role is limited to considering any possible prejudice to the interests of the French government. Witness, you'll now first be examined by Ms. Lee. Ms. Lee is counsel for the Prosecution, and you'll find her to your right. Ms. Lee, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. And thank you. On the outset, I would ask -- I had estimated half an hour for this witness. I may require possibly five to ten minutes in addition to the half an hour, and I would request leave from Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll follow how your examination develops, and then decide on whether you have another five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Great. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May we please have 65 ter number 30422, which is under seal, pulled up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Witness, as you've heard this morning, the Court has ordered certain protective measures with respect of you, and this includes the use of a pseudonym. So I will now refer to you by your name but as Witness or RM401. I ask that you take a look at this document, and can you please confirm whether this is your name and your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document, 30422, into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30422 receives number P2536, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2536 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Witness, did you provide a signed statement under oath in response to questions by the Office of the Prosecutor before the Tribunal de Grande Instance in Paris on the 3rd of March, 1998?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And in preparing to give that evidence -- give evidence here today, did you have a chance to review that statement?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: In preparation of your testimony here today, did you have an opportunity to review the statement that you had given to the Tribunal de Grande Instance?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Witness, my question was: If you had an opportunity to review it before coming here today.

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter number 30392 brought up in e-court and under seal. And while the document is being brought up, Your Honour, there is the witness's signed statement in the form of a proces-verbal given before a court of justice and we have seen similar statements from other witnesses. It is Witness R176, and his statements were admitted under P640 and P641. And I just would like to draw your attention to the fact that statement is given in a form of a response to specific questions put to the witness, and so pages 1 to 12 of the statement in both English and B/C/S contains responses given by this witness to specific questions that appear on pages 13 to 19 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, I would have, however, one question, unless you want to continue. I see that something has been attached to the statement, which I did not find.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: I -- I -- I have a -- I have difficulty hearing ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have difficulties hearing my voice or is there anything with your --

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I have difficulty hearing your voice. I don't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you use another socket, perhaps that may assist, since there's voice distortion. This may have an impact. Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you now hear me?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that, at the end of the statement mention is made of an attachment, which I did not find; a sketch by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that would be an associated exhibit to the statement which I will be tendering -- which I will be using during the course of the testimony and I will be tendering into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, okay. Usually when it's attached, I expect it to be part of the statement. But if you deal with it in that way, there's no problem. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this document to be the statement that you had given before the Tribunal de Grande Instance?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And I understand that you would like to have one clarification to the document that you would like to make. And this is in response to question number 34, which appears on page 8 in e-court for both English and B/C/S. And the question put to you was: "Is that true that during the afternoon, my men and I were forced to give up our UNPROFOR French battalion uniforms and don Serb uniforms?"

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: It is true that I was forced to put on a Serb uniform. I don't really know why. I don't know why I had to do this. And afterwards, I think that there were other people who had to put on these Serb uniforms, people who were with me, but -- but it is a little bit vague and blurred in my mind. But what is absolutely sure is that I had to put on this Serb uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And, Witness, with that clarification, if you were asked about these matters today, if you were asked the same questions, would you ask -- would you give the same answers to the answers that you had given in this statement, in substance?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And having taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm that the information in the statement is truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders this document, 65 ter number 30392, into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No additional objections beyond what we wrote in our Rule 92 ter response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30392 receives number P2537, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. May I take it that you wanted to tender it under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P2537 is admitted under seal. Yes, I see that you asked for it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And as mentioned earlier, there is one associated exhibit and it's 65 ter number 11493, which I will be using with the witness later on. And with your leave, Your Honour, I would like to read a brief public summary of this witness's evidence, the purpose of which has been explained to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Witness RM401 served with UNPROFOR in Sarajevo in 1995. The witness provides evidence that he and several other UN personnel were taken hostage by the Bosnian Serb forces on the 27th of May, 1995. The witness and nine other men from his unit were disarmed and taken to various locations in Serb-held territory, including, the Lukavica barracks. Upon arrival at the Lukavica barracks, the witness saw several other UN personnel detained by the -- by the VRS. For at least two days, the witness and other UN personnel were beaten by their captors, tied to each other and threatened with death. The witness heard a message from the VRS to UNPROFOR stating that if UNPROFOR did not heed to their request, the witness and other UN personnel would be executed. The witness and other UN personnel were released on the 13th of June, 1995. Your Honours, this concludes the summary for this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have any additional questions please put them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Lee. May I remind you that, in relation to the half an hour, you've taken already seven additional minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be very brief. I only have two different areas that I'd like to go into, and it won't take more than -- more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try to keep it as limited as possible and avoid repetitious evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you were not executed at that time and you say that you were brought back to the Lukavica barracks. Now, may I ask when was it that you -- you and your men first received food after -- since -- since you were first detained by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: We received a very small breakfast on the following morning, on the 28th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ivetic, if you are ready to start your cross-examination. Witness 401, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to first ask you some questions about the proces-verbal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which is P2537, under seal, and the same should not be broadcast to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, were you presented with the questions in written form or orally during that procedure?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: During -- in March 1998, this was in an oral form. During this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did someone meet with you prior to the proces-verbal in order to obtain preparatory information from you that would be used in preparing the questions that were presented?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Could you specify your question or make it clearer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Some of the questions appear to be fairly detailed in nature. Did someone meet with you prior to the proces-verbal in order to obtain preparatory information that would be used in preparing the questions that were to be presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it may create some confusion, Mr. Ivetic. Prior to the proces-verbal. The proces-verbal is the written version of the examination of the witness so perhaps -- did you meet with anyone to give information before you were questioned, which resulted in that proces-verbal to be drafted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We first had an informal interview, and then there was a formal interview. The proces-verbal was taken during the official interview. A judge from the cour d'appel de Paris put questions to me, and I answered his questions. My answers are contained, therefore, in this proces-verbal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Apart from the judge and yourself, who else was present for the informal interview that took place before the generation of the proces-verbal?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was the judge present during the informal interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there was a transcript or recording of this informal interview that occurred before?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes. After this informal interview, a document was drafted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps there's a misunderstanding there as well. Was there any verbatim recording of the informal interview as it is produced, for example, in this court, verbatim? Or was it audio-recorded; if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a written trace of this informal interview. Questions were first put to France, and France had accepted some of these questions, and I answered these questions. This was during the informal interview. After that, it was an informal -- it was a formal interview, and the questions were quasi-identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I ask one question in relation to one of your previous answers. You said you don't remember whether other persons were present during the informal interview. Now, we know that the formal interview, it is recorded that a person working for the Office of the Prosecution of the ICTY was present. Do you remember whether that person was present also during the informal interview and whether it was the same person, or whether there were more or other persons, or was it just that one person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. I had rather not answer this question because I could answer erroneously. I remember one particular person who gave me his or her card. I don't know if this person was there during the first interview. I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the written answers that we have in court, which have now been admitted as P2537, under seal, was that generated after the informal meeting or after the formal meeting?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: All the interviews I attended have the same content. The formal interview -- the informal interview led to the formal interview, and I stated again the same positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, it will not change any of the answers of the witness, but when I said earlier that one person is recorded as having been present at the formal interview, I looked at the French version and I overlooked that at the first line of page -- of the next page, it is recorded that a second person was present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the witness has no recollection, we don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- have to revisit it. But I would just like to put that on the record that I made a mistake there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I understand your position that the interviews had the same content. My question is: With respect to the written answers that you signed every page of, were those generated after the informal interview or after the formal interview?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I will repeat what I said in order to be more precise. Questions were sent before the informal interview to Paris. Paris accepted some questions, and I was asked these questions during the informal interview, and then the same questions were asked again during the formal interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the time of the formal interview, did you already have the typewritten answers of yourself to those questions which you signed?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Given that the answers were the same, there wouldn't have been any difference if I had have them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then could you tell us whether you had them or not?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes. These were my answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I understanding your answer to be that you did have in your possession a typewritten set of your answers to the questions before the formal interview began?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When were those answers signed? Was it before or after the formal interview?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For purposes of the formal interview, did you merely read the answers that had been pre-prepared?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Of course, I reviewed the document; but as I said when I arrived here, I stood by my answers. The unfolding of the events and what had happened to us was in line with my former answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I to understand, sir, then, that for the purposes of the formal interview, there were no questions posed and no answers given. You stood on the written answers that had been prepared outside of the formal interview?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I am not sure I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the formal interview, is it correct that you only stated that you stood by the written answers that had been prepared prior to that interview?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: At the formal interview, we, indeed, took over the main lines of the -- of the informal interview, but I added some details and some elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Ivetic -- perhaps this may clarify it. During the formal interview, were the questions again put to you? That is, did the judge read the questions again and did you then give the answers as recorded? Or how did that happen actually during that interview? Or did the judge say: Looking at question 24, would you like to add anything to what you have prepared as an answer? We're interested in -- to know exactly - Mr. Ivetic, that's at least, I think you're trying to find out - exactly how the formal interview then was conducted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The formal interview happened the following way. The judge asked me questions about what happened to me. In a chronological order, I told all the details and the different stages of the hostage-taking and the detention conditions. He did not say first question, second question, et cetera. He asked me questions, and, actually, he rephrased some of these questions, so this happened without specific preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, that about the questions. Your answers, did you refer to answers you had put on paper already, or did you really then repeat or give the answers by speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It lasted for more than one day, and I orally repeated everything that had happened to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I might put one additional question. And how was that recorded? You say it took a long time. How was that recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A courtroom registrar was there and he noted down everything. It took some time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now the -- the answers which you signed, were those the result of what the courtroom registrar had recorded or were the answers that you had in your possession -- that you had in your possession before the formal interview?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: My answers at the formal interview, since questions were basically the same as during the informal interview. During the informal interview, we had taken questions in a chronological order. We did the same during the formal interview, and I repeated my answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You said that you added some material to some answers. Are the answers that we have in court signed by you now including those additions that you made during the course of the formal interview?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say the process took over a day. How long? Was it a full second day or ...

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: The formal interview started around 9.00 a.m., and it ended around 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I note that some of the answers, for instance, number 15, page 4 in the English, page 7 in the French, page 5 in the B/C/S, begin with the text: "We note that the witness has already provided an answer to this question." Who was it that -- whose words, instead of yours, are recorded as saying this?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: The person who recorded my words was in the room along with other people in the judge's office. I cannot say more than this. The judge must have asked the question, and one of the attendees must have said: This question has already been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to move to another topic. And, again, it's dealing with the -- with this written statement that resulted. And it's answer number 6, page 3 in the English, page 5 in the French, page 4 of the B/C/S. Here, sir, you talk of a familiarisation phase before deploying to Yugoslavia. How long did this familiarisation phase last?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: The familiarisation phase before arriving on the theatre of operations can vary, depending on the nature of the operation. This is what we call operational stage. And generally, we are given information about the task itself, and then we have some practical exercises about the mission that we will have to carry out in the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now specifically focussing on the familiarisation phase that was held before your deployment to Yugoslavia in 1995, how long did that phase last?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: If I remember well - this happened more than 18 years ago - it must have lasted between two to three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During this familiarisation phase that lasted two to three months, were the Bosnian Serbs described as an actual or perhaps potential enemy or hostile force, or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: One to two months, instead of two or three months.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a theatre of operations is presented, the different factions are presented. Our mission was a UN mission. We were blue helmets, and we were an interposition force. So our role was to separate two warring factions. We were trained for that, unbiased.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could move to number 9 in your answers in the proces-verbal interview. Page 4 in English, page 5 in French, page 4 of the B/C/S. Here you state that the mission given to you by UNPROFOR was to prevent the Serbs from gaining access to the Bosnian Presidency building. What means were you authorised to employ in order to fulfil your mission to prevent the Serbs from gaining access to the Bosnian Presidency building?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Our deployment on this post was a really key point in Sarajevo, as you said. Our mission was, first of all, to interpose between Bosnians and Serbs and to prevent Serbs from taking the symbols of authority, i.e., the parliament and the Presidency building by crossing the Miljacka and the Vrbanja bridge. Our means of disposal were simply the post being there, to prevent any offensive by car in that neighbourhood of the parliament, and if the Serbs had crossed our post, we would have opened fire legitimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask for one clarification. In the written statement, it is said "the Bosnian Presidency building." You have now used the word "parliament" building. Which is correct?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: We always talked about the Bosnian Presidency building, but maybe it was the Bosnian parliament. The inhabitants of Sarajevo, or people who know more about this, could give you a clearer answer. But in any case, the symbols are what matters here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you also tasked by UNPROFOR with preventing the BiH Muslim side from gaining access to Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: As I said, and I will limit my answer to our mission, I was positioned on the line of the Jewish cemetery that you might know, between the Vrbanja bridge and the Debelo Brdo position, and our mission was to operate interposition on this line, between the two factions. I can only answer about my mission and what I did in the field in the framework of my mission. An interposition mission goes both ways, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was it part of your interposition mission to prevent the BiH Muslim side from staging attacks from their territory against the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Between the Vrbanja bridge and the Debelo Brdo position, on the posts that we held within the framework of the interposition mission, it would, indeed, have been unacceptable that any faction whatsoever could stage attacks on any side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the days leading up to the 27th of May, 1995, am I correct that your post had been caught in a cross-fire between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Serb army, just a few days earlier?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. When we arrived on May the 12th in Sarajevo, the situation was quiet. The city was relatively quiet but still quiet. And from the 16th and 17th May on, combats raged between both factions on that line of the Jewish cemetery, that is to say, between the Vrbanja bridge and Debelo Brdo. And to be completely precise, my post was fired at by mortar fire, 30-millimetre guns and LPG [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this combat that started on the 17th of May on, was it initiated by the Armija BiH?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'd like to move to the 27th of May, 1995. At number 16 of your answers in the proces-verbal - page 4 the English, page 7 in the French, page 5 in the B/C/S - you state that your post came under attack from the Serbs at 4.10 a.m. on that date. Can you please tell us what form this incoming fire took; that is to say, what type of weapons were involved?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: They did not use weapons. It was a commando operation, a rapid one, a brutal one, at night, and many people got into our post. They were dressed with UN uniforms, for some of them, and they immediately captured the two soldiers who were at the observation post facing their position, and one after the other, we were then captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct no casualties were suffered by your side from this capture?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: You are absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the time of the unit's capture, did you have anyone at your location among your fellow soldiers who was able to communicate in Serbo-Croatian with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: At the time of the capture, I voluntarily wanted to avoid a bloodshed within the observation post, and I'm the one who did not want any fire. As I already commented, the post was in darkness so that no movement could be seen from the outside. And if fire had been opened, a bloodshed would have resulted from that. We were blue helmets from the United Nations. We were on a mission under chapter 6 of the United Nations, and as far as I'm concerned, it was out of question to make any concession. I tried to contact my superiors, to tell them what was happening in the post, but the Serbs, the Serbian militiamen, pulled all the communication wires that were in the observation post, and I could not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the additional information, sir. Now, could you answer my question. Is it correct that none of you -- the French soldiers could communicate with the Serbs in Serbo-Croatian at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: The only words that were exchanged were in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, when you say you tried to contact your superiors via radio, was that your attempt to try to peacefully resolve the situation?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Had UNPROFOR instructed you how to proceed in the event that either party to the conflict took such action in capturing you or other soldiers or the observation post?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: The instructions were very clear. I mean the UN instructions. The night before, several WPCs had fallen, as I already said, so we had strengthened our observation posts. The instructions were then very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that UNPROFOR had called in NATO air-strikes prior to the 27th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: About these issues, I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Had UNPROFOR -- the UNPROFOR instructions you speak of, did they identify that NATO air-strikes were to be expected?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: As a leader, I had to operate from a tactical point of view. The tactical point of view is in the field. Above me was the operational level. Manoeuvres are designed, for instance, with all necessary support, and above that is the strategic level, including all the political and military parameters. So, at my level, at the tactical level, I can give you -- I can give you answers about the tactical situation at the Jewish cemetery, but I cannot give you any information about the operational level or the strategic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you about the instructions that you said were very clear. Did those very clear instructions include information that NATO air-strikes called by UNPROFOR were expected?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: With regard to the air-strikes, I was not aware of the expected air-strikes. What we knew was that two WCPs had been taken by the Serbs, for them to take over their weaponry. We also knew that some comrades had been taken hostage in these WCPs, and as far as our posts were concerned, we had to strengthen our protection. These were the instructions that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I want to look at number 17 of your answers in the proces-verbal. Page 5 in the English, page 8 in the French, page 6 of the B/C/S. Here you state that initially you were convinced the assailants were only militiamen, but now you state you believe a majority of them were militiamen. What I want to know is what you mean when you talk of militiamen? Are you talking about the police, which is the milicija in Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: As far as we are concerned, when I talk about militiamen, I'm talking about people who take up arms, who put a uniform on, and they put uniforms that they find on the ground, and they operate with or without uniforms, and they take part in fightings, in conflicts, next to the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so just to be clear, the assailants that took over the post, is it your evidence that they included militiamen and regular army, or militiamen and other persons?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: There were militiamen and military people from the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn for a moment to another document but please also not broadcast this to the public. This document is 65 ter number 17449.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is dated July 8th, 1995, and is a questionnaire drafted by the named UNPROFOR soldier whose name we should not mention. Looking at the name and position of this individual, but without stating his name or his relationship to you, can you tell us if you recognise or know this individual?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: You're talking about the first part? The name which is -- which appears at first? Because I can see several names on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the name of the person that appears four lines from the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have reason to believe that this individual would have access to accurate and truthful information as to the incident where you and others were taken captive 27 May 1995?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 3 of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Pardon me, page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: I'm -- may we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is not being broadcast. I would ask that we focus on the last paragraph of item number 2, which is at the bottom of the screen. And, again, I will not mention your name, but it says here that your group was captured by fanatics under the command of Slavko Aleksic, nicknamed Duke. And there is no mention of any other forces taking part in this attack and capture. Does this refresh and is it in accord with your recollections?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, absolutely. I would like to remind you that this happened at 4 -- at 10 past 4.00 in the morning, so it was still dark. This group of people acting like a commando overpowered us, and there were militiamen, irregular Serbs, but there were also people of the regular army, because when they took us from Prisunic to Lukavica, there were one or two Serbs who were with us all the time. They escorted us all the way to Lukavica and they had a Serb uniform. And I'm absolutely hundred per cent sure about that. So these might be details that the commander of the battalion is not aware of. Maybe he didn't learn about this. The majority of these commando was militiamen of Duke Aleksic, but amongst them were members of the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can take a look at another document. And, again, this should also not be broadcast. 65 ter number 17724. And we only have the B/C/S and the French. I'm working off the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And item number 4, which is on page 1 of both the French and the B/C/S, indicates that during the capture your captors treated you well. Is that in accord with your recollections?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. When I answered this questionnaire, and I'm just putting things back into their context, this was written when I reached Split after I was released. So as I was saying, this was written once I had been released. And you cannot disassociate things. What I mean is that after what we went through from the morning of the 27th of May until the following morning, and I'm talking about, generally speaking, during our detention, we were well treated. Of course, we had been captured whilst we were in our post, and this was a first problem. And blue helmets had been made prisoners. There was no physical violence, or no important physical violence, as opposed to what happened during the course of the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look again at item number 4 in both the B/C/S and the French, it states here that the persons who captured you prevented you from making contact with the UN. Is this a reference to the same incident at the observation post where the wires were ripped from the radio that you mentioned earlier, or is this another incident?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: No, we're talking about the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I'd like to turn to your proces-verbal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: P2537, under seal, should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I, meanwhile, ask a question clarifying the last answer. You told us that when they entered, you tried to contact your superiors and that they made that impossible. Did, at any point in time later - for example, being in Lukavica - did you ask to be allowed to contact your superiors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In Lukavica, I did not ask to contact my superiors. In Lukavica, I didn't manage to get in touch with my superiors, because people in Lukavica were totally cut off from the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And knowing this, you did not ask for an opportunity to contact your superiors. Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not get in touch with my superiors to tell them that the post had been taken over by Serbs. I could not do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also not any higher-up authority of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can turn to P2537, under seal. Page 6 in the English, page 10 in the French, page 7 of the B/C/S. The response to question number 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here, you are talking about an officer who came to the Prisunic building and then later in Lukavica. And it says: "One of the two men asked me for my radio frequency with a view to making contact with my superiors and I refused. I understood ... he was distinctly put out by my response." First of all, sir, was this person who asked you for the radio frequency that you refused the request, was he a member of the regular Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was this request of you for the frequency made at Prisunic building or Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: In the Lukavica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, we have talked about how you wanted to make contact via radio with your superiors to alleviate the situation, and now when a Serb army officer is asking you for the frequency to effectuate such contact you refuse. Can you explain to me why you refused such contact that might have served to alleviate this volatile situation?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Well, it's very simple. I did not have to give the radio frequencies that we were using. This was just a question of protection for the forces. In fact, this could have been -- if I'd given the radio frequencies, it could have run counter to the mission. I wanted to be on top of the situation. I wanted to control the situation. I wanted to get in touch with my superiors, but I didn't want to other people to use our radio frequencies in order to get in touch with them. I wanted to be in charge. I was a prisoner -- well, not. I wasn't a prisoner, in fact. I was a hostage. But I referred to the Law on Armed Conflicts, which means that you give your name, your first name, your date of birth, your grade, and your unit, and that's all. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Isn't the -- the instructions to give your name, your date of birth, your grade, and your unit, isn't that in relation to prisoners of war, sir?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And this is the -- how paradoxical was the situation. I was a blue helmet for the UN, and I ended up as a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we're at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. Ivetic. We first turn into closed session so as to allow the witness to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ivetic, once the noise has disappeared, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like next to move to number 30 of the proces-verbal, which is page 7 in the English, page 11 in the French, page 7 of the B/C/S. And, sir, here, you state that your: "... guards acted in a strange manner towards us. On some occasions they were well behaved; on others they were aggressive." Did it seem to you like the guards did not know what to do with you?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I think that they knew what to do with us because they were guarding us. But on the other hand, I'm not sure that they knew which behaviour to have towards us. So it is true to say that their behaviour was rather strange, as I have indicated. Sometimes they were violent. At other times, they were calm in order to reassure us. I have no explanation about the -- this very contradictory behaviour towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is, again, still on the 27th of May. Would it be fair to say that on that day, both Serb civilians and the Serbs in uniform appeared upset and distraught, not only over the NATO air-strikes but over the deaths of Serbs in the UN recapture of the observation post?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: It's difficult to answer this question. Were they dissatisfied or angry because there were two dead people and four wounded people when our unit recaptured the post? We also suffered two dead and 17 injured. Or is it -- or were they like this because the negotiations were failing and they didn't manage to get back their dead, their wounded people, and the captured people?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge of the fact that forward air controllers capable of guiding the NATO air-strikes to their targets were embedded with various UNPROFOR and UN units on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I didn't know that. And I don't know whether this is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were any of the men in the same unit as you with sufficient training and NATO credentials to act as forward air controllers?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: You asked me a question about air controllers, but they did not belong to our units, so I cannot answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, my second question was in relation to the men in your unit, whether they had training and NATO accreditation to act as forward air controllers.

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Absolutely not. This is a skill that we did not have, but we were rather well trained in order to comply with our mission. The -- and I'm talking about the interposition mission that was ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point, sir, either during your captivity or thereafter, learn that the International Red Cross had proclaimed that you and other UNPROFOR men should be regarded as prisoners of war because of the acts undertaken by UNPROFOR of calling in NATO air-strikes against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: I would like to have the foundation of this information or a source of this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I -- I -- most of the -- most of the law review articles on the topic reference it. I didn't think it was a disputed fact that the ICRC had made such a proclamation. I'm asking the witness if he knows of it. I'm not going to rely upon it as positive proof without bringing other witnesses and other evidence, but that is the foundation of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could be a bit more precise. Most of the law review articles on the topic. I take it if the position of the ICRC is invoked, that there is a source for the ICRC expressing itself on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, I think we have a source for the [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if the witness -- if the witness never heard about it, then it's irrelevant whether -- so, therefore, Witness, before we further explore the basis for the question, did you ever learn about an ICRC position that you should be regarded as prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, still, the basis for the question, I think it would be fair, Mr. Ivetic, if you would inform Ms. Lee about it so that if the same question would come up anywhere in the future, that she would know what the basis for it was. And, meanwhile, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can at the moment refer to an article by Lieutenant-Colonel H. Wayne Elliott of the JAG Corps, retired in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before, it is irrelevant at this moment. If you would reveal that information to Ms. Lee, then the purpose of it is served sufficiently for this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, did it appear to you, sir, that the -- that the Serb soldiers at Lukavica barracks were undertaking to protect you from harm, including protecting you from both Serb civilians and so-called militiamen?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I don't know. They were assigned to guard us - no more, no less - in these barracks. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While in the barracks, did they prevent civilians from coming in contact with you?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Yes, they did. When we had our daily meals, let's say, in an area of the barracks, civilians had their meals also, but we were never in contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned the daily meals. Is it correct during the entirety of your stay at Lukavica barracks you ate the exact same food as did the Serb soldiers at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I would like to seek a clarification of one of the previous answers. You were asked whether they did prevent civilians from coming in contact with you. Your answer was that there was no contact, and you referred to the daily meals. Did you gain the impression that those civilians that were there would have been hostile so as to be prevented from having any contact with you? In other words, did you consider the fact that no contact was allowed or made to be in order to protect you against those civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could return to the proces-verbal at number 31, which, I believe is on the screen in both languages. For the record that would be page 7 in English, page 11 in French, page 8 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you describe that some high-ranking Serb soldiers came to visit you, although they were not wearing any combat gear so as to permit to you identify their rank. How is it, then, that you were able to discern that these were high-ranking officers rather than ordinary officers, or someone else, if you could not discern their rank?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: When I talk about combat gear, I'm not talking about battle dress. They were wearing uniforms, but they were not in combat gear. They were wearing shirts and trousers but not in battle dress. Let's say, these were uniforms they wore when they wanted to go out and one could identify them thereby. These people were of a certain age and had a certain authority. I saw them at a meeting, and they were discussing things. So I can say that these were people with a high level of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is that merely based upon their age and the fact that you believed them to be officers of unknown rank?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I state that these were high-ranking officers. They were not wearing battle dress, like what can be seen in war operations. These were staff officers who were wearing uniforms, and that's why I can say that these people were high-ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at number 42 of the proces-verbal. That is at page 9 in the English, page 14 in the French, page 9 of the B/C/S. And this is the incident you talked of where you were forced to kneel in the middle of the road. First of all, sir, this is all still happening before you were taken to Lukavica barracks and taken into possession by the regular army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: We were forced to kneel at that time, but I state that at that particular location, which was close to a square, militiamen were present. There were soldiers of the regular army that were there, and a host of civilians that was there also.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I -- I understand that, sir, and I believe that's contained in your written statement. My question is: Was this before you were transferred into the custody of the regular army at Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: This occurred before we were transferred to Lukavica. What I would like you to understand is that when we were in this negotiation phase and when the negotiations had floundered, these things were tied together. In the building where we were detained, there were militiamen who were guarding us. There were these staff officers of the regular army that there were too. This was to-ing and fro-ing, incessant to-ing and fro-ing in this building. And when we went down and were forced to kneel down before our UN post and before the Bosnian sector, the militiamen, the civilian population, and the regular army were all connected to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph number 43 of the proces-verbal, which is on the same page in the English and the French and the B/C/S, too, I believe, you state that the crowd showed hostility toward you. Are you here talking about the civilians, the mixed group of militia and regular army that that were at this square, or are you talking about only specific elements of them?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I mean everyone. Tensions were running very high. People were screaming, were shouting. The attempted exchange failed. We were at a time when the French vehicle had brought back these two dead Serb people. When the bridge was taken back, you can imagine that when the soldiers, the civilians, and the families came to fetch the bodies, the two bodies, you must understand that everybody was in a highly tense state, and people were mad at us. You can imagine that perfectly well, can't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and we'll get to that. I'd like to now move to -- to the question -- or to the answer number 46 of the proces-verbal - page 10 in English, page 15 in French, page 10 of the B/C/S - and, first of all, sir, the French-speaking woman whom you describe here, how would you describe her knowledge of the French language? Was it fluent in nature or basic, rudimentary, in nature?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: She spoke French extremely well. That struck me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this answer number 46 of the proces-verbal, you say that you "now recall." What was it that caused you to recall that she said you were to die. Why had that not been recalled earlier?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Could you rephrase your question more clearly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The last paragraph of number 46 of the proces-verbal states -- and I will not use the names, of course, states: "In fact, I now recall that she indicated that," and she mentions a name, "and I were to die and that I was to designate two other individuals." What caused it to -- for you to now recall such a significant fact?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I'm trying to put my -- to return to that formal interview as opposed to the informal interview. As I said earlier, when I came to the formal interview, I provided more details. My answers were more accurate. This is undoubtedly due to the fact that a request had been put to me. I remember this now, today, but you can check in the -- in the informal interview, I have always said that I had been designated, and I was to die, and I had drawn up a macabre list of people who were to die.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the -- in the information report arising from your proofing with the Prosecution yesterday, the Prosecution reports as follows, and I will not use the -- neither your name, nor the name of the position. But it says: "On 27 May 1995, during the collection of Serb bodies from," and then it names the post, "the witness was told that if anything went wrong during the process, he would be released into the Bosnian front lines while wearing the Serb army uniform." Does that version from the proofing session you had the past few days with the Prosecution more accurately depict what, in fact, transpired during this occasion?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: As regards this particular incident, the Serbs had told me that: In any case, if things go wrong, you will be released on the Bosnian front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, so, sir, were you told that you would be shot or that you would be released towards the Bosnian lines? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, while this all is going on, isn't it a fact that prior to this instance, that is to say, when the Serbs encountered casualties and the French encountered casualties in taking over the post, isn't it correct that the UNPROFOR forces participated in joint combat with the Armija BiH to take over that check-point, thus causing the casualties among both the French and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: That's totally wrong. I have had a lot of questions about that particular issue. The French blue helmets just re-took the post they had lost, and our president of the republic gave an order for that. We had been humiliated for long enough. We needed a striking fact and the Vrbanja bridge was the pretext. We wanted the blue helmets to be considered legitimate. And what the Bosnians do -- did when they re-took the bridge was an action which was undertaken by them and by them only. That decision was theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just intervene for one second. Mr. Ivetic, you're held holding the paper at such a position that it can be caught by the cameras, which is to be avoided. So would you please -- I take it that you were unaware of that, but could you please leave them on your desk. I interrupted you. Apologies for that. You said: "... it was an action which was taken by them and by them only. That decision was theirs." Could you please resume from there. And could Mr. Mladic remain seated and speak at a low --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- seek leave to consult briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's be polite and first --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: After the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- ask the witness to complete his answer and then you have an opportunity to consult, Mr. Ivetic. You said it -- that action was theirs and theirs only. Did you want to add anything to that when I interrupted you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At no point in time - I wish this to be very clear - were the Bosnians informed about the fact that the bridge had been re-taken. They noticed this when French soldiers started infiltrating and moving towards the bridge. They realised then that something was happening and that some action was undertaken. Because on the other side of the Miljacka, the river, we had established armoured support to control the takeover of the bridge. We did not need the help of the Bosnians to take back the bridge. The Bosnians benefitted from this action --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you also to slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Bosnians benefitted from this action, and then -- let me remind you that the Bosnians were never informed about our desire to take back the post, and we never turned to them for support or help. What they initiated, they initiated themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you have an opportunity to consult with Mr. Mladic if you wish to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Low voice, please. Low voice, please. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, again, according to the information report given to us by the Prosecution resulting from the last two days of meetings that you've had with them, it is recorded as follows, and I will, of course, edit out the names involved, but it reads: "Two French soldiers were killed during the re-taking of the Vrbanja bridge," and then it names them. "17 other French soldiers were wounded. The ABiH assisted the UNPROFOR in the retaking of the," and then it names the post. "At that time, the UNPROFOR and the ABiH were not aware that two French soldiers," and then it names them, "were present in the post." Then it says that: "One of the French was wounded in the knee by support fire by the ABiH." Sir, is everything that I've just read you to the truth?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: The Bosnian army started shooting when the Vrbanja bridge was re-taken - that's a fact - which made the fire more intense, of course, but I challenge the fact that this was a joint operation. You can't deny the fact that they shot at the post while we were re-taking it. We have a proof of that. There was a stray bullet that wounded (redacted) (redacted) tendered mentions the fact that this injury might have been caused by the Bosnians. No one at the post was aware of the fact that two French soldiers were still manning the post. They were hostages --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: They were not manning the post. They were hostages of the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I told you, I was unable to contact my superiors to describe them what had happened at the Vrbanja post.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so at that time, prior to the threats being issued to you, prior to you being forced on your knees, the combined crowd of civilians, Serb soldiers and Serb militiamen, as you call them, had witnessed the French forces taking the check-point with the ABiH forces offering support fire and assisting the French, causing Serb casualties. That all happened before the threats that occurred that you testified about. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: First of all, I -- I believe it is fair to ask the witness whether or not he is aware if the crowd of civilians of Serb soldiers and militiamen witnessed the French forces taking the check-point back, because that statement has been put to him. And I think it is only fair to the witness to ask him whether or not he was aware of that and then the subsequent question could be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand there's a request to split up the question, including the part that the combined crowd of civilians had witnessed the French forces taking the check-point. Would you please split it up, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that this crowd of mixed civilians, soldiers, and militiamen had witnessed the re-taking of the check-point and the support fire by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether they had seen the post being taken over. I myself was unaware of it. I heard about it in the afternoon. I inferred that that must have been the case. And then when we moved into the negotiation phase for a potential exchange, what happened in Grbavica is something I know nothing about it. I don't know what people knew about it and I don't know how much they knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the re-taking of the check-point, the support fire from the ABiH and the casualties resulting therefrom had all occurred before there were any threats to your life, whether to execute you or to release you to the Bosnian army positions?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, this happened before. But the casualties on the French side, the wounded on the French side, and the casualties on the Serbian side and the dead people on the Serbian side was -- happened because a UN bridge had initially been taken by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can focus on your proces-verbal at number 48, which is on page 10 in the English, page 16 in the French, page 11 of the B/C/S. And again, this is where you say that at Lukavica you were read the Geneva Conventions by the Serb commander. Can we mark this as the first time in the proces-verbal where you felt or understood yourself to be in the custody of the regular Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: When the Geneva Conventions were read, I first was surprised in my head because I thought, Hmm, I'm a blue helmet, and I'm a prisoner. There's something wrong here. And then I thought that I was no longer, along with my fellow soldier, in that hell we experienced on the Vrbanja bridge. We were in a more quiet and peaceful environment. So you can imagine how we felt at that moment. We were quite reassured, actually. We were reassured because we had escaped this hell that we were in during 24 hours on the Vrbanja bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At Lukavica, at the time that the Geneva Conventions were being read to you, isn't it also correct that the Serb officers explicitly stated that they regarded you as prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I remember very well this officer who told us, You are going to be treated according to the Geneva Conventions, and he added that we would be treated as prisoners of war, yes. Maybe it was a bit too late to mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move to number 50 in the proces-verbal, page 11 in the English, page 17 in French, page 11 of the B/C/S. And, first of all, I'd like to focus on the first incident on the 29th of May, 1995, the other men that you learned had been taken away and filmed handcuffed to military equipment. First of all, did you ever learn or did they tell you what kind of military equipment this was?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: On May 29, two of my soldiers were, indeed, taken away to be filmed near some equipment. I don't know which equipment it was exactly. They did not report that to me. They did not tell me the type of equipment they had been handcuffed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you how long approximately they had been handcuffed to such equipment? Was it a matter of minutes, dozens of minutes, hours, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: It was very, very short. And then these images were relayed around the world, in newspapers, on television, to put pressure on the international level about this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the time that they were very shortly handcuffed, is it correct that there were no actual ongoing air-strikes in their immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And they were uninjured and unharmed when they returned to be rejoined with the rest of you at Lukavica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I want to focus on the second incident in answer number 50 to the proces-verbal, that is, the 30th of May, 1995, when two other men were taken for the same purpose and you served as the English interpreter for the same. First of all, am I correct that you yourself were not handcuffed to any structures or equipment? It was just these two other men?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, 1995, were these two men beaten or mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ivetic, same as before. We wait until the noise disappears. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to again focus on the 30 May 1995 second incident in answer number 50 of the proces-verbal. These two men that were affixed to a military structure or equipment, how long did they remain affixed to the military structure or equipment in question?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: A few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What kind of military equipment or structure were they affixed to for those few minutes?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, during the few minutes that these two men were handcuffed to whatever it was they were handcuffed to, am I correct that there were no actual air-strikes in that area in their immediate vicinity at that time?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking now at number 51 of the proces-verbal, which is at page -- it's the same page in both the French and the English, and page 11 of the B/C/S. Can we conclude that, apart from these two incidents which we have now described, there were no other incidents where you witnessed men being taken away from Lukavica to be handcuffed to equipment or structures and taped -- or filmed?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: These are the only two moments when my men were asked to follow the Serbs to be filmed. The only two moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could focus on number 54 of the proces-verbal, and that's on page 12 in both the English and the B/C/S, page 18 of the French. And this is the visit from the Serb Orthodox priest that you mentioned. Did he have a translator or were you able to speak directly to him in a language that you understood?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: The visit of the Orthodox priest happened in English. He had no interpreter. And one of my soldiers who was fluent in the language acted as an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say one of the soldiers who was fluent in the language, are we talking about English or Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- ask one clarification. I think earlier you said you served as an interpreter for - let me see - it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Number 50, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 50. I'm just -- you said you served as an interpreter and you gave responses. What language did you serve as an interpreter? French/English or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, French/English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I added, I do not speak English fluently, and I acted as an interpreter for those people. But when the Orthodox priest came to visit us, since the conversation was longer, I was helped by one of my men who was fluent in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you speak English, but you preferred here to be assisted by someone who better speaks English. Is that -- yes. It was a bit surprised by at one moment serving as an interpreter yourself and then -- but let's leave that aside. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And during the course of your stay at Lukavica barracks, did you get the impression that the regular Serb army did not condone of the treatment that you had received during the first day from those men of Duke Aleksic who had captured you and held you during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: When we were in detention at the Lukavica barracks, the people who guarded us and us had polite relations. At no time they told us what they thought about the men of Duke Aleksic, and at no time we told them what we thought about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you happen to know the -- with -- in respect to the Serbian Orthodox priest, was he just a priest or was he a higher official? Did you have any further information of where he came from?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: I had no information. He introduced himself as an Orthodox priest. He was wearing the insignia of the Red Cross. He told us that he represented the Red Cross, and he said that as -- in this capacity he came to visit us. At no time he introduced him and told us the details about his rank within his church.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that this priest who introduced himself as from the Red Cross, when you say that you received correspondence, would it be correct to say that he had correspondence that had been written directly -- specifically for yourselves as recipients from -- from -- from -- from persons outside of the -- from back -- back -- from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: The Orthodox priest gave us letters. Among the letters was one letter from my superior. I think, but I'm not sure about that, I think that there were also letters from our relatives. I don't remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you say that you were released and went via Pale and Belgrade, during that travel, is it correct that you were not mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for your patience in answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Ms. Lee, any requests in re-examination? I take it from what you told us earlier that you have a few.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes. And I would require about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Witness, you were -- you were just asked during cross-examination about any mistreatment that you have -- you and your men may have received on the 30th of May, 1995, and I refer you to transcripts 64, lines 17 until 65 and line 4. And this was -- and this was in relation to your men who were being handcuffed to equipment and structure. And we've heard more evidence on that just now on pages 67 and 68. And I would like to just read you the question that was put to you, and it was at -- line 64, 17 says -- 64, line 17, and it says: "My question had been specifically related to the 30th of May, 1995, when two men were taken with you acting as the English interpreter to a site, a factory near Lukavica, and were handcuffed to something there." And the question put to you was: "On that date, is it correct that neither you nor those other two men who -- were beaten or mistreated in any other way?" And then it was said: "I'm not talking about the time-period prior." And you responded: "Yes, we were not beaten then." What -- my question to you, Witness, is: The fact that you were handcuffed to military equipment, do you consider that to be a mistreatment or not?

utterances.speaker: RM401
utterances.text: Yes, this is part of mistreatment. That's obvious. I'm sure that you have understood that I'm talking about a global event. It is the same event, the taking over of the Vrbanja bridge. And I compare what happened afterwards with what had happened during the 27th of May. So, sure, we were handcuffed to -- we were handcuffed, we were tied to military equipment. This is not acceptable, of course. But compared to what we had gone through during the 27th of May, this was a better treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I proceed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter number 30424 on the screen and not to be broadcast because this is a statement that this witness had given, and we have heard evidence about the statement earlier today. It is the informal statement. And -- and if I could have page 5 and focus on paragraph 5 near the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
